newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Philips cuts Grundig stake to 5 percent.
newsitem.headline: Philips cuts Grundig stake to 5 percent.

text.p: Philips Electronics NV said Friday it reduced its 31.6 percent stake in Grundig to 5 percent, distancing itself further from the struggling German television and audio equipment maker.
Philips said it sold the 26.6 percent stake to an investor group led by privately owned London-based merchant bank firm Botts and Co. Ltd.
A spokesman said the move followed the company's decision this year to stop covering Grundig's losses and move to a passive shareholding.
"Taking into account the decision we took at the beginning of the year, it is a logical further step to reduce our interest in Grundig," said Philips spokesman Ben Geerts.
Philips added that it was disputing the 671 million mark ($374 million) 1996 losses reported by Grundig.

It said the stated loss had been inflated by extensive provisions for new policies adopted after the year end. This view was shared by a report from Arthur Andersen, but Philips had not reached a settlement with Grundig.
"Philips will therefore ask the court to nullify Grundig's 1996 annual accounts," Philips said.
"The consideration of the shares depends on the realisable future value thereof," Philips said in a statement.

At the heart of Philips' troubled relationship with Grundig is a deal struck in 1984 in which Philips agreed to pay an annual dividend to Grundig and to buy 52 percent of the company for 411 million marks in 2004.
"We won't take the initiative to reopen negotiations. That means that in 2004, they will execute their put option to sell the 52 percent to us. We would sell it further," said Geerts.
"They have the right to exercise their put option in 2004, we tried to get a settlement but without success," he added.

"As from the beginning of this year we became a passive minority shareholder and we're still in that position with 5 percent. We continue to view Grundig as a valued business partner, only we have conflicts about the magnitude of the 1996 losses," Geerts said.

Analysts welcomed the move by Philips to tackle one of its principal loss-makers -- part of the strategy kicked off by Chairman Cor Boonstra when he vowed late last year to deal with "bleeders" and underperformers.
